_about: The evaluation dataset: real questions from the developer who will use the knowledge base, written before the pipeline exists so every stage can be measured against them.
Questions keep their original casual style and typos - 'waht is stock exchange' tests the query rewrite on purpose.

expected_sources were located in the loaded text on 2026-09-28 (phase 1). pdf_page is the page a PDF viewer opens; printed_page is the number printed on the page (OpenStax: pdf_page - 14). Wikipedia sources carry the indexed revision. 'confidence' is how sure the locating was that this passage answers the question; 'confirmed' is true once the operator has checked the question: q01-q14 were confirmed on 2026-09-28 from the phase 1 report. q15-q24 were added on 2026-09-29 (the operator's questions, q24 proposed by the pipeline's author and chosen by the operator; sources located the same day); all confirmed by the operator the same day. q25-q29 were added on 2026-10-01 (the operator), q30 (a prompt injection) proposed by the pipeline's author the same day, mainly to give 'not found' more than one question; three of the operator's proposals were left out because they border the held-out set (an indicator formula next to h09, timeframes next to h08, versioning next to h10).
Never put source text in this file - references only. It is tracked.

The expected behaviour is relative to the corpus. A question the corpus cannot answer stays in the dataset with behaviour answer_not_found - 'nothing found' is a correct answer, and the question marks a gap for extending the sources.

How an expected source is matched (phase 3): the document by 'source' (and 'article' for Wikipedia); the section by 'anchor' where the entry has one (null = the article's lead, which has no anchor), otherwise by 'section', the section title as indexed.

i01-i30 were added on 2026-11-06: questions from the coding sessions of a project that consumes this knowledge base, written from the needs in its own open and closed issues; not by the operator, nor by the pipeline's author. Each expected source was confirmed by reading its page on the search server, then mapped by the pipeline's author to what the index holds for it (a PDF page to its outline unit, an HTML section to its anchor, a Wikipedia section to its article and anchor). 'style' (title_words, keywords, short_phrase, question, section_paraphrase) and 'found_by_search' (the keyword search's rank of the expected page for the question as written, or null) come from the authors. A reviewing agent gave ten of them a second reading the same day (i03, i07, i11, i12, i15, i16, i19, i23, i26, i30): nine were amended, each saying what and why in 'amended'; i19 had been marked not found and is answerable in part. 'confirmed' stays false until the operator has checked them.

q31 was added on 2026-11-10 (the operator's question in chat, verbatim, decision 151.a), after the runs phases 6 and 7 report: those measured 60 questions, and q31 is measured from the next run on. Its sources were located and confirmed by the operator the same day (decision 152.a).

behaviours.answer_direct: one concept, one or two precise section references
behaviours.answer_broad: several aspects, several sections, possibly from both shelves (trading/finance and architecture)
behaviours.answer_general: a coarse question; a short explanation plus an entry-level section, or say plainly that the corpus holds specialist material only
behaviours.answer_partial: the corpus covers the topic only partly; answer what it covers and say what it does not
behaviours.answer_not_found: the corpus has nothing on the topic; say so plainly instead of answering from the model's own knowledge, and flag the topic as a gap in the sources
behaviours.clarify: too vague to answer well; ask one focused follow-up question, optionally with a short orientation
behaviours.decline_off_topic: outside the domain; decline before any retrieval is paid for, friendly, optionally with an offer of what the knowledge base can do
behaviours.decline_harmful: a request for something illegal or harmful (breaking into systems, cheating a broker, market manipulation); decline plainly and give no hints, before any retrieval; at most one sentence pointing to a legitimate reading of the question (added 2026-09-29, a domain security measure)

questions.question: explain arbitrage to me using BTCUSD
questions.expected_answer: What arbitrage is and when it is possible (the law of one price violated, e.g. the same BTCUSD quoted differently on two exchanges), why it is not free money in practice (execution or leg risk, capital tied up), and why it matters less today (low-latency arbitrage is HFT territory). The BTCUSD example is an illustration built on the sourced conditions, marked as such; crypto specifics are not in the corpus - say so briefly.
questions.correction: the operator's note: arbitrage matters less than it used to, because of advanced trading networks, but good approaches keep appearing - one of the most solid strategies if you are patient. The first part is right and the corpus supports it (low-latency arbitrage profits of over US$21 billion a year, all HFT). The second needs care: classic arbitrage is about speed, not patience, since the gap closes quickly. The patient variant is pairs trading or statistical arbitrage, waiting for prices to converge, and there the corpus says convergence is not guaranteed and the strategy can lose for years (2004-2007). Crypto adds costs the corpus does not cover: transfer times and fees between exchanges, and exchange counterparty risk.

expected_sources.note: law of one price; simultaneous buy and sell across exchanges; leg-in and leg-out risk; never a free position in practice
the definition: a risk-free profit at zero cost, in theory
low-latency arbitrage as an HFT business; statistical arbitrage
the patient variant: convergence is not guaranteed

questions.question: how can i get around the swap fees at my broker
questions.expected_answer: A legitimate question. Swap is the interest on positions held overnight, so the plain way around it is not to hold a position over the daily rollover. Otherwise, in forex it cannot be avoided, only chosen: some brokers offer swap-free accounts (usually with other fees instead), and a carry trade can even earn swap. Or choose a different market.
questions.correction: the operator's expected answer was 'in forex you cannot avoid swap; otherwise choose a different market'. That holds for positions held overnight, but two legitimate ways are missing: closing before the rollover (no overnight position, no swap), and swap-free accounts. The corpus covers the mechanism (overnight interest, tom-next, cost of carry, carry trades); swap-free accounts are not in it (0 hits, 2026-09-29).
